## Requirement

Build a Tier 2 Case-escalation notification path: when a Case moves into the existing Tier_2_Engineering queue, an Apex Queueable (enqueued off the escalation-triggering automation, authenticated via a Named Credential + External Credential holding the on-call tool's API key) posts case number, severity, subject and a case link to an HTTPS on-call-tool webhook with status-code-based retry, and the same escalation publishes a Platform Event that an already-subscribed internal ops dashboard consumes; every delivery attempt lands on a new, admin-visible failure/audit record with a manual resend action, and the API key is held only in an External Credential, never in code or a Custom Setting.

## Scope

### In scope

- Detect a Case whose owner changes to the Tier_2_Engineering queue, in an after-update context, and act within a minute of the save (requirement para 1; Q9, Q13).
- POST one JSON notification per escalated Case to the on-call tool's HTTPS REST endpoint, carrying case number, severity, subject and a link back to the Case (requirement para 1; Q1, Q30, Q31).
- Authenticate that call through a SecuredEndpoint Named Credential over a separate External Credential with a named principal, so the API key never appears in code or a custom setting (requirement para 4; Q2, Q3, Q4, Q5, Q6, Q25).
- Classify the response: retry 429/502/503/504 and connection timeouts up to three times with backoff; write the failure record immediately on 400/401/403/404/422 (requirement para 2; Q7, Q15).
- Send an Idempotency-Key header built from the Case Id and the escalation timestamp so a retry cannot double-page (Q8).
- Publish a Tier2_Escalation__e platform event with PublishAfterCommit for the external ops dashboard, and check the publish result rather than assuming delivery (requirement para 2; Q10, Q11, Q12, Q39).
- Create Integration_Failure__c with the diagnostic field set Q18 names, the restricted Status and Severity picklists Q17 fixes, and a Resend checkbox (requirement para 3; Q16, Q17, Q18).
- Stamp Case.Tier2_Notified_At__c when the webhook succeeds, and skip a Case already stamped inside the last ten minutes, so a re-save does not re-page (Q14).
- Grant the External Credential principal and Integration_Failure__c CRUD/FLS through a Tier2_Webhook_Admin permission set (Q19, Q20, Q23).
- Re-send a failed notification when a Support Engineering admin ticks Resend on the failure record (requirement para 3; Q20).
- Run an hourly channel-health check that emails Support Engineering when more than three failures land in an hour, or when no success has occurred in 24 hours while escalations exist (Q24).
- Ship every artefact in one build-level package.xml with a written deploy order, including the Apex members the apex-builder steps cannot manifest themselves (Q25; standards/build-orchestration.md section 5, The Apex exception).

### Out of scope

- Any customer-facing change. The requirement states 'No customer-facing change' and Q44 confirms the audience is internal employees only, with no Experience Cloud or partner licence implication; nothing in this plan touches a site, a customer-visible layout or an external email.
- The ops dashboard's Pub/Sub API subscriber, its authenticating principal, its IP allowlisting, its login-hour policy and its service-account ownership. Q32, Q33, Q34, Q35 and Q37 each record the subscription as already established and owned by the dashboard's own team.
- Salesforce-side deduplication of the escalation event. Q12: the dashboard team dedupes on case number plus escalation time and accepts duplicate events, so no dedupe is built here.
- Outbound Message / Workflow Rule mechanics - WSDL version, sending user, includeSessionId and the dead letter queue permission. Q26, Q27, Q28 and Q29 are all moot once Q2 rejected Outbound Message in favour of a Named-Credential Apex callout.
- An in-Salesforce report or dashboard on notification failure rates. Q45: none requested beyond the external ops dashboard the platform event feeds.
- Creating or changing the Tier_2_Engineering queue and the escalation rule that fills it. The requirement's closing paragraph states the existing case-intake build already provides them and this build may assume the queue exists (see assumption A8).
- Verifying the org-wide email address support-noreply@acme.example. Q24 records it as a deploy prerequisite, and skills/admin/email-templates-and-alerts states that org-wide email addresses have no metadata type, so nothing in this build can deploy or verify it (see assumption A4).
- Flow-based alternatives for the triggering automation and their fault routing. Q40, Q41 and Q42 are each conditional on choosing Flow, and decision D8 chose Apex.
- Apex managed sharing, sharing rules or a criteria-based rule on Integration_Failure__c. Decision D12 settles record visibility with a Private OWD plus an object-scoped grant on one narrow admin permission set instead.

## Decisions

| Id | Decision | Decision tree | Branch | ADR | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `D1` | Salesforce calls out to the on-call tool fire-and-forget from a Queueable implementing Database.AllowsCallouts; nothing calls into Salesforce for this feature. | `standards/decision-trees/integration-pattern-selection.md` | Q1 |  | Q1's answer confirms Direction 1 only and Q9 confirms no user waits on the result, which is exactly this branch. Continuation is excluded because nobody watches a spinner; Batch is excluded because the volume is 15 a day peaking at 50 in five minutes (Q22). |
| `D2` | Authenticate with a Named Credential over a separate External Credential using the Custom authentication protocol, with the API key injected as the X-API-Key header by the credential rather than by Apex. | `standards/decision-trees/integration-pattern-selection.md` | Q2 |  | Q6 names X-API-Key as the tool's documented header and Q5 assigns header ownership to the platform, so generateAuthorizationHeader is deployed false and the header is an ExternalCredential AuthHeader parameter. Apex sets no credential header at all, so allowMergeFieldsInHeader stays false. |
| `D3` | The External Credential declares a NamedPrincipal, not a PerUserPrincipal, and the Named Credential is the enhanced SecuredEndpoint type rather than Legacy. | — | — | ✔ | integration-pattern-selection.md Q2 routes to 'Named Credential + External Credential (Custom)' but does not choose between principal types or between the legacy and enhanced models; the skill's Decision Guidance does, on both counts - 'Async job (Batch / Queueable / Scheduled) -> NamedPrincipal' and 'every legacy field is deprecated at 56.0 - new work goes on SecuredEndpoint'. Q3 and Q4 answer the same way. |
| `D4` | The webhook body is JSON, serialised and deserialised in Apex through templates/apex/HttpClient.cls rather than a hand-built HttpRequest. | `standards/decision-trees/integration-pattern-selection.md` | Q3 |  | Q1 and Q6 both describe a JSON POST. Q31 sizes the payload well under the 6MB/12MB ceilings, so no paging or chunking is needed. |
| `D5` | Transient failures (429, 502, 503, 504 and connection timeouts) are retried up to three times by re-enqueueing from the Finalizer with a MinimumQueueableDelayInMinutes backoff; 400, 401, 403, 404 and 422 write the failure record immediately with no retry. | `standards/decision-trees/integration-pattern-selection.md` | Q4 |  | Q7 supplies the classification table verbatim. skills/apex/apex-queueable-patterns bounds the pattern: the delay caps at 10 minutes and a Finalizer may re-enqueue a failed job five consecutive times, so three attempts sits inside both ceilings. HttpClient.retryOnTransient is deliberately off because its backoff is a busy-wait that burns Apex CPU. |
| `D6` | Every webhook POST carries an Idempotency-Key header built from the Case Id and the escalation timestamp captured at enqueue time. | `standards/decision-trees/integration-pattern-selection.md` | Q4 |  | Q8 confirms the tool accepts an Idempotency-Key header and names the Case Id plus the escalation timestamp as the key. The tree's 'tie to Request_Id__c' is adapted: this build has no Request_Id__c and the same string is stored on the failure record instead, so a resend replays the identical key. |
| `D7` | A Queueable Finalizer, attached as the first statement of execute(), is what guarantees the failure record is written - including when the job dies on a limit or unhandled exception. | `standards/decision-trees/async-selection.md` | Q7 |  | Q15 requires the failure record on every terminal state. skills/apex/apex-queueable-patterns is explicit that try/catch cannot survive a limit exception that terminates the transaction and that the Finalizer runs either way, with FinalizerContext.getResult() returning SUCCESS or UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION. |
| `D8` | The escalation-detection automation is Apex - a Case after-update trigger delegating to a handler and a service layer - not a record-triggered Flow. | `standards/decision-trees/automation-selection.md` | Q3 |  | Q3's list is satisfied on two counts: callouts that need retry and backoff, and a deployable unit under an enforced coverage gate with assertion-style tests. The tree's own note that 'one straightforward callout is NOT on this list' does not apply - the classification table in Q7, the Finalizer, the idempotency key and the resend path are the opposite of straightforward. Q13 also places the enqueue in the after-update handler's service layer. |
| `D9` | The ops dashboard is fed by a Tier2_Escalation__e platform event it consumes through the Pub/Sub API, not by a second direct callout or an internal service call. | `standards/decision-trees/async-selection.md` | Q11 |  | The requirement states the dashboard is a separate system already subscribed to Salesforce platform events, and Q39 confirms no internal Apex or Flow subscriber exists. The tree's delivery-allocation note applies: an API subscriber draws on the 24-hour delivery allocation, and 15 escalations a day is far inside it. |
| `D10` | Tier2_Escalation__e is declared with publishBehavior PublishAfterCommit and is published from the escalating transaction's service layer - before the Queueable runs - rather than from inside the Queueable's execute(). | — | — | ✔ | Q10 requires that a rolled-back escalation reach neither the on-call tool nor the dashboard, which PublishAfterCommit gives directly. The sequencing half is not in any tree: skills/apex/apex-queueable-patterns states that callouts are impossible after DML in the same transaction, and a publish-after-commit publish is a DML statement, so publishing inside execute() before the callout would break the callout. Publishing in the trigger transaction also means the dashboard sees the escalation regardless of webhook outcome, which was Q9's proposed sequencing default. Q11 requires the publish SaveResult to be checked and a failed publish logged to the same failure object. |
| `D11` | The hourly channel-health check is Schedulable Apex whose execute() only enqueues a Queueable, not a schedule-triggered Flow. | `standards/decision-trees/async-selection.md` | Q2 |  | Q24 delegates the choice to this tree, and standards/decision-trees/README.md assigns Schedulable-versus-Scheduled-Flow to async-selection.md rather than to automation-selection.md or flow-pattern-selector.md. The cadence is the reason it does not fall out to Flow: flow-pattern-selector.md Q6 gates a schedule-triggered flow on a daily, weekly or monthly cadence, and this is hourly. The library also disagrees with itself on whether a scheduled flow can run hourly at all - skills/flow/flow-time-based-patterns says it can, skills/flow/scheduled-flows says the granularity may not fit - which is a second reason not to build on it. |
| `D12` | Integration_Failure__c ships with a Private org-wide default, and the three Support Engineering admins get every row through object-scoped View All Records / Modify All Records on the Tier2_Webhook_Admin permission set rather than through a sharing rule. | `standards/decision-trees/sharing-selection.md` | Q1 |  | Q19 and Q20 answer CRUD/FLS and the resend owner but not record visibility. The tree's Q1 rules out shipping a Public Read/Write default; its 'Permission sets vs sharing' table then places this case - 'Can user bypass sharing to do admin things?' - on View/Modify All at object scope, to be used for narrow admin permission sets, which Tier2_Webhook_Admin is. A criteria-based sharing rule was rejected because the criterion would be 'every row', which is a whole-object grant wearing a rule's clothes. |
| `D13` | Cross-transaction duplicate suppression uses the Case.Tier2_Notified_At__c stamp with a ten-minute window, not AsyncOptions.DuplicateSignature. | — | — | ✔ | Q14 chose this mechanism explicitly. The skill's own canonical answer to the same question is DuplicateSignature, which suppresses across transactions where a static guard cannot; it is recorded as the rejected alternative rather than silently dropped. The field stamp was chosen because it is also the audit trail an admin reads on the Case, and because a suppressed DuplicateSignature enqueue throws DuplicateMessageException rather than no-op'ing, which would need its own catch. |
| `D14` | Tier2_Webhook_Admin is assigned to every user who can escalate a Case to Tier 2 and to the user who schedules the hourly health check, because the Queueable calls out as the user whose save enqueued it and scheduled Apex runs as the user who scheduled the job - neither is the Automated Process entity. | — | — | ✔ | Q23 asserts the Automated Process entity and asks the plan to settle how it gets the principal grant. The skill states that async Apex runs as the async context user - the user who fired the async, except for scheduled jobs and platform-event triggers - and skills/flow/flow-and-platform-events records that Automated Process holds no profile and no permission set assignments, so the grant Q19 describes cannot be made to it at all. skills/apex/apex-named-credentials-patterns is the matching rule from the credential side: the permission set must be assigned to the user the transaction runs as, which for Queueable Apex is not necessarily whoever started the work. The same rule settles M1-S04: skills/apex/apex-user-and-permission-checks names the scheduler as the running user for a scheduled job, so the scheduling user needs the same permission set for read on Integration_Failure__c and on Case.Tier2_Notified_At__c. That user is inside the assignee set only if they can also escalate a Case, which nothing guarantees, so the set is stated as the union of the two rather than left to coincidence. |

- `D1`
  - Branch quote: ├── No, fire-and-forget → Queueable with AllowsCallouts
  - Alternatives rejected: Continuation; Batch Apex; Outbound Message on a Workflow Rule; @future(callout=true)
  - Consequences: The notification is decoupled from the save, so a webhook outage never blocks a Support agent's escalation - and the only evidence a notification failed is the Integration_Failure__c row this build creates.
- `D2`
  - Branch quote: ├── Custom header / API key → Named Credential + External Credential (Custom)
  - Alternatives rejected: API key in a Custom Setting or Custom Label; Apex-built Authorization header with an Apex-side {!$Credential.*} merge field; Basic auth
  - Consequences: The secret is entered in Setup against the principal after deploy and is never in source, an export, or a sandbox refresh - which also means the deploy alone does not make the integration work: a human must enter the value and assign the permission set.
- `D3`
  - Source reference: `skills/apex/apex-named-credentials-patterns/SKILL.md`
  - Alternatives rejected: PerUserPrincipal; Legacy Named Credential with an embedded endpoint and protocol
  - Consequences: One shared service identity means the on-call tool's audit trail attributes every incident to Salesforce rather than to the escalating agent; the trade is that a per-user principal would not work from a Queueable at all.
- `D4`
  - Branch quote: ├── JSON REST → HttpClient + JSON.serialize/deserialize
  - Alternatives rejected: Raw HttpRequest construction in the Queueable; SOAP; form-encoded body
  - Consequences: The endpoint, the timeout and the retry switch are all set through one builder the checker recognises, which is also why the per-Case callout loop does not trip check_callouts_and_http_integrations.py rule 4.
- `D5`
  - Branch quote: ├── Known 429 throttling → Queueable with exponential backoff + Finalizer
  - Alternatives rejected: HttpClient.retryOnTransient(true); a hand-rolled retry loop inside execute(); retrying every non-2xx status
  - Consequences: A permanent failure surfaces in under a second rather than after three pointless retries, and a 401 never becomes a lockout - but anything needing more than three attempts or more than ten minutes of backoff is out of this pattern and lands in the failure record as Abandoned.
- `D6`
  - Branch quote: ├── Idempotency key required → Generate in Apex, send as header; tie to Request_Id__c
  - Alternatives rejected: No key, accepting a possible double-page on an ambiguous 5xx; a random UUID per attempt; the AsyncApexJob Id
  - Consequences: A retry after an ambiguous transport failure cannot page twice; the cost is that the key must be captured once at enqueue and carried through every retry rather than recomputed, which is what assumption A10 records.
- `D7`
  - Branch quote: ├── Yes → Use a Queueable Finalizer to dispatch the compensating action
  - Alternatives rejected: try/catch inside execute() alone; a platform event published from the catch block; relying on AsyncApexJob.NumberOfErrors for visibility
  - Consequences: The Finalizer runs in its own transaction under synchronous governor limits, so it must stay thin - it records and re-enqueues, and does not do the work over again.
- `D8`
  - Branch quote: ├── Yes → Apex (trigger + handler + service layer)
  - Alternatives rejected: After-save record-triggered Flow with an InvocableMethod callout action; Flow plus an Apex invocable per automation-selection Q6; Outbound Message
  - Consequences: Apex carries a 75% org-wide coverage gate Flow does not, and the fault path is a failure record this build owns rather than a Flow error email - which is also why Q40, Q41 and Q42 are out of scope.
- `D9`
  - Branch quote: ├── Yes → Platform Event + Pub/Sub API gRPC subscriber
  - Alternatives rejected: A second HTTP callout to the dashboard; Change Data Capture on Case; an internal Apex service call
  - Consequences: Delivery is at-least-once and the dashboard dedupes its own duplicates (Q12); EventBus.publish returning success means queued, not delivered, which is why D10 requires the SaveResult to be inspected.
- `D10`
  - Source reference: `skills/apex/apex-queueable-patterns/SKILL.md`
  - Alternatives rejected: Publish inside the Queueable before the callout; publish inside the Queueable after the callout, carrying the callout outcome; PublishImmediately
  - Consequences: The event carries no callout outcome - the dashboard learns that an escalation happened, not whether the page landed - and a failed publish is a separate Integration_Failure__c row from a failed webhook.
- `D11`
  - Branch quote: ├── Clock (cron) → Schedulable wrapper that enqueues Queueable
  - Alternatives rejected: Schedule-triggered Flow; Batch Apex; a Flow scheduled path on Integration_Failure__c
  - Consequences: Schedulable Apex runs under synchronous governor limits and cannot call out, which is fine for two aggregate queries and an email, and the CRON literal makes the hourly cadence explicit and deployable rather than a Setup-time choice.
- `D12`
  - Branch quote: ├── Public Read-Only / Public Read-Write → Tighten OWD before adding anything → Q2
  - Alternatives rejected: Public Read/Write OWD; criteria-based sharing rule; Apex managed sharing; View All Data on the permission set
  - Consequences: The grant is object-scoped and auditable in one named set, and check_permission_set_architecture.py reports it as a sharing-bypass WARN by design rather than as an error; the trade is that anyone holding Tier2_Webhook_Admin sees every failure row including its stored request payload.
- `D13`
  - Source reference: `skills/apex/apex-queueable-patterns/SKILL.md`
  - Alternatives rejected: AsyncOptions.DuplicateSignature built from the Case Id; a static in-transaction guard alone; no dedup
  - Consequences: The window is wall-clock rather than transactional, so two escalations of the same Case eleven minutes apart both page - which is the intended behaviour - and a Case whose webhook never succeeded is never stamped, so it is never suppressed.
- `D14`
  - Source reference: `skills/apex/apex-user-and-permission-checks/SKILL.md`
  - Alternatives rejected: Assigning the permission set to the three admins only; granting the principal to the Automated Process entity; moving the callout into a platform-event-triggered subscriber so it does run as Automated Process
  - Consequences: The assignee list is wider than Q19 anticipated - every user who can escalate, plus the scheduling user - and is an access decision a human signs at the M1-S02 gate. If it is wrong the failure is loud rather than silent: every escalation returns 401 and lands in the failure record, and the hourly check throws on the first query. Assumption A2 carries the library's own hedge on the word 'often' and A13 carries the scheduling-user half.

## Milestones

### M1 — Tier 2 escalation notification, event and failure record, deploy-ready

Goal: Given a Case whose owner changes to the Tier_2_Engineering queue, when that save commits, then a Tier2_Escalation__e event is published for the ops dashboard, the on-call tool receives one authenticated JSON POST carrying case number, severity, subject and a case link, Case.Tier2_Notified_At__c is stamped on success, any failure leaves an Integration_Failure__c row a Support Engineering admin can see and re-send from, an hourly job reports a dark channel, and every component is listed in one package.xml with a written deploy order.
